title: Close Reading & Textual Analysis
description: Learn to read extracts closely — analysing word choice, imagery and sentence structure — and turn your observations into critical paragraphs that link technique to meaning.

notes.heading: What is Close Reading?
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Close reading is the slow, careful examination of a short piece of text to understand how its language creates meaning. Instead of asking only what a text says, it asks how and why it says it that way.

🔑 Key Concept
• Read short passages more than once — first for meaning, then for method.
• Assume every choice is deliberate: words, images, sentence lengths, punctuation.
• Move between the tiny (a single word) and the whole (the writer's purpose).
• The goal is interpretation, not summary.

💡 Worked Example
'The gate hung open.' A surface reading notes an open gate. A close reading asks why 'hung' — a passive, slightly wrong word that suggests neglect or that someone left in a hurry.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Quality of attention matters more than quantity of text.
• Observations must be tied back to meaning and effect.
• There is rarely one 'right' reading — but every reading needs evidence.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Retelling what the extract says instead of analysing how it works. If your sentence just paraphrases the text, it is not yet analysis.

notes.heading: Word-Level Analysis & Connotation
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning; connotation is the set of associations and feelings it carries. Word-level analysis examines why the writer chose this word and not a near-synonym.

🔑 Key Concept
• Compare near-synonyms: 'slim', 'thin', 'gaunt' and 'skeletal' share a denotation but climb from complimentary to disturbing.
• Notice semantic fields — clusters of words from one area (war, illness, money) that colour a passage.
• Single verbs and adjectives often carry the most weight.

💡 Worked Example
'The frost crept along the windowpane.' 'Crept' (rather than 'spread') connotes stealth and threat — the cold moves like an intruder, making the house feel besieged.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always name the specific word you are analysing, in quotation marks.
• Ask: what does this word make me picture or feel that its synonyms would not?
• Connotation is about shared associations, not wild personal guesses.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'the writer uses the word X' without saying anything about it. Naming a word is selection, not analysis — you must explain its effect.

notes.heading: Imagery and Its Effects
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Imagery is language that appeals to the senses or that describes one thing in terms of another — similes, metaphors and personification. Analysing imagery means explaining what the comparison adds.

🔑 Key Concept
For any image, ask three questions:
• What is being compared to what?
• What qualities does the comparison transfer?
• Why is that effect right for this moment in the text?

💡 Worked Example
'Homework piled up like snowdrifts.' Comparing homework to snow suggests it is cold, heavy, accumulating and eventually burying the speaker — the image turns a chore into something suffocating.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• 'It creates an image in the reader's mind' is not analysis — say what kind of image and why it matters.
• Images can work together across a passage to build a pattern.
• Consider what the image reveals about the narrator's attitude.

✅ Check
Can you complete this sentence about the image? 'The writer compares ___ to ___ in order to suggest ___.'

notes.heading: Syntax and Sentence-Length Effects
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Syntax is the arrangement of words and sentences — their length, order and structure. Writers shape syntax to control pace and emphasis.

🔑 Key Concept
• Short sentences — create pace, tension, finality or shock. They land like blows.
• Long, multi-clause sentences — build atmosphere, mirror overwhelm or let a thought unfold slowly.
• Lists — suggest abundance, chaos or obsession.
• Questions and exclamations — mimic a mind under pressure or address the reader directly.
• Fronting — putting a key word first ('Gone was the bridge') adds emphasis.

💡 Worked Example
'He ran. The alley narrowed. Somewhere behind him, a door opened, and footsteps — quick, unhurried, patient — began to follow.' The short sentences tighten the pace; the long final one slows dreadfully, mirroring the pursuer's patience.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Link sentence form to content: pace, panic, calm, confusion.
• A sudden change in sentence length is usually significant — notice it.
• Punctuation (dashes, semicolons, ellipses) shapes rhythm too.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'the short sentence makes it dramatic' for every short sentence. Be specific: dramatic how — abrupt, breathless, shocking?

notes.heading: The Unseen-Extract Method
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The unseen-extract method is a repeatable process for analysing a passage you have never seen before, under time pressure.

🔑 Key Concept
Follow five steps:
• Read — once for basic meaning: who, what, where, what changes.
• Notice — read again, annotating striking words, images, sentence shapes and shifts.
• Select — choose three or four of your strongest observations, not every annotation.
• Analyse — zoom into the exact words and explain their connotations and effects.
• Link — connect each effect to the extract's bigger meaning or the writer's purpose.

💡 Worked Example
Given an extract about a heatwave, you might select a personified sun ('the sun interrogated the streets'), a list of wilting details, and a final one-word sentence — then link all three to the writer's picture of a city under siege by weather.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The selection step is where most marks are won or lost — pick evidence you can say a lot about.
• Keep the question or theme in view at every step.
• Timed practice makes the method automatic.

✅ Check
After annotating, can you say in one sentence what the extract is doing overall? If not, read again before selecting.

notes.heading: Building a Critical Paragraph
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A critical paragraph argues one point about how a text works, supports it with evidence, and explains the effect. A common structure is Point, Evidence, Analysis, Effect.

🔑 Key Concept
• Point — a clear claim answering the question, not a plot statement.
• Evidence — a short, well-chosen quotation, embedded in your own sentence.
• Analysis — zoom into specific words or techniques within the quotation.
• Effect — explain the impact on the reader and the link to the text's wider meaning.

💡 Worked Example
'The writer presents the city as hostile. The sun is said to "interrogate" the streets — a verb from the semantic field of policing, which casts the heat as an aggressive authority figure. This makes the reader feel the city offers no escape, reinforcing the extract's mood of entrapment.'

📎 Key Points to Remember
• One point per paragraph; depth beats breadth.
• Keep quotations short — a phrase is often enough.
• Verbs like 'suggests', 'implies' and 'evokes' keep analysis tentative and precise.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dropping in a quotation and moving on. A quotation without analysis is evidence for nothing.

notes.heading: Common Pitfalls in Textual Analysis
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Pitfalls are habits that make analysis look busy while saying little. Recognising them in your own work is the fastest way to improve.

🔑 Key Concept
• Feature-spotting — naming a technique ('the writer uses a metaphor') without explaining its effect.
• Retelling — summarising what happens instead of analysing how it is written.
• Vague effects — 'it makes the reader want to read on' or 'it paints a picture' could be said of anything; be specific.
• Overclaiming — 'this proves' or 'clearly shows' when the evidence only suggests.
• Technique-hunting — writing about an obscure feature you barely understand instead of an obvious one doing real work.

💡 Worked Example
Weak: 'The writer uses alliteration in "dark, dripping doorway" which is effective.'
Stronger: 'The repeated d-sounds in "dark, dripping doorway" thud dully, echoing the slow dread of approaching the house.'

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Every technique you name must be followed by 'which suggests...' or 'so that...'.
• Specific beats impressive: a plain word analysed well beats a rare term analysed badly.
• Re-read each sentence and ask: could this be written about any text? If yes, sharpen it.

✅ Check
Highlight every technique name in your paragraph. Is each one followed by a genuine effect? Delete or fix any that are not.

flashcards.definition: The slow, careful examination of a short text to understand how its language creates meaning.
flashcards.example: Reading a ten-line description three times to study its word choices, images and sentence rhythms.

flashcards.definition: The associations and feelings a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning.
flashcards.example: 'Home' connotes warmth and safety; 'house' is emotionally neutral.
The denotation of 'slim' and 'gaunt' is similar — not having much flesh — but their connotations differ.

flashcards.definition: A cluster of words in a text that all belong to one area of meaning, colouring the passage.
flashcards.example: 'Interrogated', 'searched' and 'cornered' form a semantic field of policing and pursuit.

flashcards.definition: Language that appeals to the senses or describes one thing in terms of another, including simile, metaphor and personification.
flashcards.example: 'The cold snapped at her fingers' is an image making the weather feel hostile.

flashcards.definition: The arrangement of words and sentences — their length, order and structure.
flashcards.example: Three short sentences in a row can quicken the pace before a sudden revelation.

flashcards.definition: Brief sentences create pace, tension, emphasis or finality by delivering information in sharp units.
flashcards.example: 'He ran. The alley narrowed. Then: silence.'

flashcards.definition: Multi-clause sentences slow the pace, build atmosphere or mirror a mind overwhelmed by detail.
flashcards.example: A single sentence listing everything in a cluttered attic mirrors how the clutter overwhelms the narrator.

flashcards.definition: A conclusion drawn from evidence in the text rather than stated directly.
flashcards.example: A character folding a letter 'smaller and smaller' lets us infer anxiety.

flashcards.definition: A short quotation woven into your own sentence rather than dropped in separately.
flashcards.example: The gate 'hung' open, a passive verb that suggests long neglect.

flashcards.definition: Naming a technique without explaining its effect — a habit that earns little credit.
flashcards.example: Writing 'the writer uses a metaphor here' and moving straight on.

flashcards.definition: The specific response — feeling, image, judgement — that a language choice creates in the audience.
flashcards.example: The abrupt final sentence jolts the reader, mirroring the shock the character feels.

choices: What happens in the text?
How and why does the language create its meaning?
Who wrote the text and when?
Whether the text is true
questions.explanation: Close reading moves beyond content ('what happens') to method — how word choice, imagery and structure produce meaning and effect.

questions.stem: What is the connotation of a word?
choices: Its dictionary definition
Its spelling and pronunciation
The associations and feelings it carries beyond its literal meaning
The number of syllables it has
questions.explanation: Connotation is the halo of associations around a word — 'home' and 'house' denote the same thing but connote very differently.

questions.stem: In a Point-Evidence-Analysis-Effect paragraph, the 'evidence' is usually:
choices: Your personal opinion
A short quotation from the text
A summary of the whole passage
The writer's biography
questions.explanation: Evidence means a brief, well-chosen quotation that supports the point — ideally embedded in your own sentence so you can zoom into its wording.

choices: Finding every metaphor in a text and explaining each one
Naming a technique without explaining its effect
Reading a text more than once
Choosing the best quotation for your point
questions.explanation: Feature-spotting is identifying a device and stopping there. Analysis only begins when you explain what the technique makes the reader think or feel.

choices: A list of difficult vocabulary at the back of a book
A cluster of words in a text that all belong to one area of meaning
Any field described in a poem
The punctuation pattern of a paragraph
questions.explanation: A semantic field is a group of words drawn from one area — war, illness, money — whose repeated presence colours the whole passage.

questions.stem: In 'The frost crept along the windowpane', why is 'crept' more effective than 'spread'?
choices: It is a longer word, so it looks more academic
'Crept' connotes stealth and threat, making the cold seem like an intruder
'Spread' is grammatically incorrect here
'Crept' tells us the exact temperature
questions.explanation: Word-level analysis compares near-synonyms: 'crept' carries associations of sneaking and menace that 'spread' lacks, which makes the house feel under threat.

questions.stem: 'He ran. The alley narrowed. A door opened.' The main effect of these short sentences is to:
choices: Slow the pace so the reader can savour the details
Create a quickening, breathless pace that mirrors the character's panic
Show that the writer could not write longer sentences
Introduce a flashback
questions.explanation: Short sentences deliver information in sharp bursts, speeding up the rhythm and echoing the panic of the chase. Specific effect beats the vague 'it adds tension'.

questions.stem: 'Homework piled up like snowdrifts.' What does this simile most strongly suggest?
choices: The homework is white and cold
The homework is accumulating until it buries and traps the speaker
The speaker enjoys winter sports
The homework will melt soon
questions.explanation: Analysing imagery means asking what qualities the comparison transfers: snowdrifts accumulate and bury, so the image makes the workload feel suffocating and inescapable.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best example of an embedded quotation?
choices: The text says the gate hung open. This is a quotation.
'The gate hung open.' (line 4)
The gate 'hung' open — a passive verb suggesting long neglect.
In this extract there is a quote about a gate.
questions.explanation: An embedded quotation weaves a few words into your own sentence and immediately analyses them. Option C quotes economically and gets straight to the effect.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of steps in the unseen-extract method?
choices: Select → read → analyse → notice → link
Read → notice → select → analyse → link to meaning
Analyse → read → link → notice → select
Link → analyse → select → notice → read
questions.explanation: You must understand the passage first (read), gather observations (notice), choose the best evidence (select), examine it closely (analyse), and only then connect to overall meaning (link).

questions.stem: Why is 'the writer makes the reader want to read on' a weak analytical sentence?
choices: It uses the wrong tense
It is a vague effect that could be said of any text, with no link to the specific language used
Readers never want to read on
It is too long to embed in a paragraph
questions.explanation: Strong analysis names a specific effect tied to specific words. 'Makes the reader want to read on' explains nothing about how this particular language works.

questions.stem: Read: 'The sun interrogated the streets. Windows shuttered themselves against it. Nothing moved; nothing answered.' Which analysis is strongest?
choices: The writer uses personification and short sentences, which are effective techniques
The sun is personified as a hostile authority through 'interrogated', and the fearful silence of 'nothing answered' presents the city as a population too cowed to respond
The passage is about hot weather and uses descriptive language to describe it
The writer uses the word 'streets' to show that the scene is set in a street
questions.explanation: Option B zooms into a specific word ('interrogated'), explains its connotations of hostile authority, and links the silence to an overall meaning — the full move from word to interpretation.

questions.stem: A writer describes a hospital corridor in one long, breathless sentence listing doors, signs, smells and sounds, then ends the paragraph with 'Maya stopped walking.' The sudden short sentence most likely:
choices: Fills up the page to reach a word count
Mirrors the chaos of the hospital with no particular contrast intended
Cuts against the overwhelming flow, snapping the reader's focus onto Maya's fear at the moment it becomes too much
Shows the writer prefers variety for its own sake
questions.explanation: A change in sentence length is significant: the long sentence mirrors sensory overload, so the abrupt short one lands like a stop, focusing everything on the character's reaction.

questions.stem: Which statement about analysing connotation is most accurate?
choices: Connotations are fixed rules every reader must agree on
Connotations are shared cultural associations, so your reading must be plausible and supported — but it need not be the only valid one
Connotation only applies to adjectives
You should always write down the dictionary definition first and stop there
questions.explanation: Connotation works through shared associations rather than private guesses, and texts are open to interpretation — but every reading must be anchored in the evidence.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The writer uses alliteration in "dark, dripping doorway" which is very effective.' What is the main problem with this sentence?
choices: The quotation is too short
Alliteration never appears in prose
It names the technique but never explains what the repeated sounds actually do
It should mention the writer's name
questions.explanation: This is feature-spotting: the sentence identifies alliteration and asserts it is 'effective' without saying how the d-sounds shape the mood. Adding the effect would make it analysis.
